title: Snake and Ladder
summary: A simulation-style case study about decoupling board rules from the turn loop, and making the board data instead of code.

slides.markdown:
Snake and Ladder feels like a five-minute script — roll a die, move a token, done. The trap is designing it that way: as one loop that special-cases every rule inline instead of a system where rules are data the loop never has to know about.

The interview signal here isn't a data structure trick, it's whether you decouple **board rules** (where snakes and ladders live) from the **turn loop** (whose turn it is, roll, move). Get that separation right and every later extension — more dice, power cards, a bigger board — costs you almost nothing.

Think of the board as a lookup table from position to position, not a grid you walk cell by cell.

**In scope:** a board of fixed size (default 100 cells), a single die, a configurable set of snakes and ladders (each a start and end position), 2+ players taking turns, first to land exactly on the final cell wins.

**Non-goals** unless asked: betting or wagering mechanics, animated token movement, and networked play. The one rule worth stating explicitly up front: does landing past the final cell count, or must a player roll the exact number to finish? Most interviewers want the **exact-roll rule** (overshoot doesn't move the player) — confirm it rather than assuming.

Naming the overshoot rule as a requirement, not an afterthought, heads off the most common pitfall in this topic (§ pitfalls).

Five entities. **Board** holds size and the snake/ladder lookup — nothing about turns. **Dice** produces a roll (1-6, or more later). **Player** holds a name and current position. **Jump** represents one snake or one ladder as a `(start, end)` pair. **Game** owns turn order and drives the loop.

The deliberate omission: **`Board` does not know whose turn it is, and `Game` does not know how jumps resolve.** `Board` answers one question — "if a player's raw roll lands them at position X, where do they actually end up?" — and nothing else. That single-responsibility split is what keeps the turn loop from ever special-casing a snake or ladder.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a turn's flow through the system
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: sequence diagram of one turn — Game asks Dice.roll(), adds the result to the Player's current position to get a raw position, passes that raw position to Board.resolvePosition() which looks up any Jump and returns a final position, Game updates the Player's position and checks for a win >>>

Notice every arrow points one direction: `Game` calls `Dice` and `Board`, but neither calls back into `Game`. That keeps board rules and turn orchestration independently testable — you can unit-test `Board.resolvePosition` with zero knowledge of whose turn it is.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: composing a turn from separate calls
The hard part: the loop never special-cases a jump
slides.markdown:
The naive design writes `if (newPosition is a snake head) { move to tail } else if (newPosition is a ladder bottom) { move to top }` directly inside the turn loop. That's a leak: the loop now knows about board content, and every new rule (a second ladder type, a portal, a trap tile) means editing the loop again.

The fix is `Board.resolvePosition(rawPosition)`, called **unconditionally on every single turn** — including turns that land on an ordinary empty cell, where it's just a no-op lookup that returns the same position. The loop treats "landed on a snake" and "landed on nothing" identically; it just asks the board where you ended up and trusts the answer.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: resolving a position through the jump map
Design patterns: one Jump concept, no State for turns
slides.markdown:
| Decision | Pattern | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Snakes and ladders | **Unified `Jump`** — a signed-offset `(start, end)` pair, no separate `Snake`/`Ladder` classes | The board doesn't care about the *direction* of movement, only the mapping — one lookup replaces two type hierarchies |
| Turn order | **No pattern** — a simple index rotation (`currentPlayerIndex = (currentPlayerIndex + 1) % players.size()`) | Turn order is a rotation with no guarded transitions or per-turn behavioral differences — a State machine would model complexity that doesn't exist |

**How to decide:** if two "different" concepts (snake, ladder) reduce to the same data shape and the same operation, model them as one type — don't let naming from the real world (snake vs ladder) dictate your class hierarchy.

Board size, every jump's start/end, and the overshoot rule should all load from **configuration** — a JSON file or a constructor argument — never as hardcoded constants scattered through `Game` or `Board`.

This matters for a concrete reason beyond "it's cleaner": it's what makes the design testable and reusable at all. A unit test wants a tiny 10-cell board with one ladder, not the full 100-cell layout; a variant board (§ deep-dives) wants different jump positions entirely. If jump positions are `if (position == 16) return 6;` scattered across the codebase, none of that is possible without editing source.

This is the same discipline the [Open/Closed Principle](ocp-open-closed) argues for generally: configuration changes, code doesn't.

A real `Dice` returns a genuinely random 1-6 every call, which makes writing a deterministic unit test impossible — you can't assert "after this exact sequence of rolls, the player is at cell 42" if the rolls themselves are random.

The fix is designing `Dice` as an interface from the start: production code uses a `RandomDice`, tests inject a `FakeDice` (or a seeded PRNG) that returns a scripted sequence — `[3, 5, 6, 2]` — so the test can assert an exact game trace deterministically.

This is a small design decision (one interface) that pays for itself the moment you need to reproduce a bug report: replay the same seed and you get the same game.

slides.sectionTitle: Extending the rules without touching the loop
slides.markdown:
Multiple dice, "roll again on a 6," and multiplayer-skip power cards are all variations the brief names — and none of them should require editing `Game.playTurn()`.

Multiple dice or "roll again" logic belongs in `Dice` (or a thin wrapper around it) — it decides how many total pips a turn produces, and whether that turn repeats. A skip-power-card belongs in a rule layer consulted before movement — it can veto the whole turn. In every case, `Game.playTurn()` still just asks "how much do I move" and "where do I land," without an if/else for each new rule.

The test for good design here: can you describe the new rule to `Dice` or the rule layer alone, with zero sentences starting "and then in `Game`, also change..."?

A local, same-screen game has no concurrency question at all — one thread, one turn at a time, nothing to design around.

An online version is different: two players' clients could both submit a roll-request for what they each believe is their turn, especially over a flaky connection with retries. The fix is the same shape as tic-tac-toe's: serialize every turn through a single **authoritative game-state actor** (one process or one row-level lock per game) that only accepts a roll from the player whose turn it currently is, and rejects or ignores a second concurrent roll for the same turn. The board and dice logic stay exactly as designed — only the entry point gets a turn-ownership check.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: one Jump concept vs two separate classes
slides.markdown:
| | One `Jump` class | Separate `Snake` / `Ladder` classes |
|---|---|---|
| Board lookup | One map, one lookup path | Two maps, or one map plus a type check on every resolve |
| Adding a new jump type (portal, trap) | New `Jump` instance, zero new code | New subclass, new lookup, new branch in `resolvePosition` |
| Readability | Slightly less "self-documenting" — `start`/`end` don't say "snake" | Reads naturally as domain vocabulary |

**How to decide:** favor the unified model whenever the *behavior* is identical and only the *label* differs — the extensibility win compounds every time a new jump-like rule shows up, and it will.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: hardcoding board layout in Game
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "It's a fixed 100-cell board with fixed snakes — I'll just hardcode the positions as constants in `Game`."

**Why it's wrong:** it works for exactly one board. The moment the interviewer asks for a smaller test board, a different layout, or a variant game (§ deep-dives), hardcoded constants mean editing and redeploying code instead of loading a different config. It also makes `Game` responsible for board content, re-coupling the exact two things §6 separated.

**Correct model:** board size and jump positions are constructor/config input to `Board`. `Game` never sees a raw position number tied to a specific layout — it only calls `board.resolvePosition(...)`.

**Wrong belief:** "If the roll takes a player past the final cell, just cap their position at the final cell — close enough."

**Why it's wrong:** most Snake and Ladder rulesets require an **exact roll** to finish — landing past cell 100 means the player doesn't move at all that turn. Capping at 100 instead silently lets a player win one or more turns early, which is a game-breaking correctness bug, not a cosmetic one. It's also the single most commonly-missed rule in this topic, precisely because it's easy to assume rather than confirm.

**Correct model:** `resolvePosition` checks `rawPosition > finalCell` first and returns the player's *unchanged* position — the turn passes with no movement at all.
